title: Economy and reference: cumulative review
objectives: Select a clear summary noun for an earlier event.
Apply ellipsis and substitution in context.
Review nominalisation, apposition and article choice.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A concise text avoids repeating information that readers can recover, while still making every important reference clear. Substitution, ellipsis, apposition and nominalisation can all reduce repetition. They do different jobs: a substitute stands for another expression, ellipsis leaves recoverable material out, an appositive adds a description, and a nominalisation packages an action or quality as a noun.

The aim is not to remove as many words as possible. A shorter sentence can force readers to guess what this, it or one refers to. Use a more explicit phrase when several earlier ideas could plausibly be meant.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: A summary noun can clarify a broad reference: “The panel postponed the vote. This decision gave members more time.” This decision points to the postponement. Compare “The panel postponed the vote after the budget changed. This caused concern.” This could refer to either event; the writer can specify “This postponement” or “The budget change” according to the intended meaning.

Agreement helps establish a clear link. “The findings were unexpected. These results changed the discussion” uses plural these with plural results. “The decision was unexpected. This decision changed the discussion” uses singular this with singular decision. A summary noun should accurately describe what happened rather than silently changing its meaning.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Earlier units showed how one and ones can replace countable nouns: “The red folder is full; the blue one is empty.” A short auxiliary can avoid repeating a verb phrase: “The team has checked the files, but I haven’t.” A nominalisation can make an action the topic of the next sentence: “They revised the plan. The revision reduced costs.”

An appositive can add a compact identification: “Mina, the editor, approved the text.” Article choice also contributes to reference: “Education matters” makes a broad claim, while “the education she received” identifies a specific experience. These patterns work best when their connection to surrounding sentences is easy to interpret.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Avoid assuming that this always refers to the nearest noun or to the entire preceding sentence. Readers use meaning and context; if two interpretations are plausible, name the intended event. Likewise, “one” usually refers to another member of the same type, while “it” normally refers back to the same identifiable item.

Nominalisation can improve cohesion, but a chain of abstract nouns can obscure the actor and the action. Appositives and reduced clauses can also create ambiguity if attached to the wrong noun. Read the passage as a whole and check whether the shorter version preserves the original meaning.

examples.note: This decision identifies the postponement as the topic.

examples.sentence: The budget changed and the vote was postponed. The postponement caused concern.
examples.note: The summary noun specifies which event caused concern.

examples.sentence: The findings were unexpected. These results changed the discussion.
examples.note: These agrees with the plural noun results.

examples.sentence: The red folder is full; the blue one is empty.
examples.note: One substitutes for a singular countable folder.

examples.note: The repeated verb phrase is omitted after the auxiliary.

examples.note: Revision packages the action as a noun.

common_errors.incorrect: The findings were unexpected. This results changed the discussion.
common_errors.correct: The findings were unexpected. These results changed the discussion.
common_errors.reason: Use these with the plural noun results.

common_errors.incorrect: The red folder is full; the blue ones is empty.
common_errors.correct: The red folder is full; the blue one is empty.
common_errors.reason: One substitutes for the singular noun folder.

common_errors.incorrect: Their analysis the figures took a week.
common_errors.correct: Their analysis of the figures took a week.
common_errors.reason: The noun analysis commonly takes an of-phrase.

summary: Use summary nouns to make references to events explicit.
Ellipsis and substitution reduce repetition when the context is clear.
Preserve agreement, meaning and the intended referent.

option_feedback.d: “This postponing of voting it” does not fit here. This decision can summarise the panel’s act of postponing the vote.
